lines: Why did one narrow waterway become central to the United States and Iran conflict in 2026? The Strait of Hormuz connects global oil markets. Let's map its geography.
The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman. Iran lies to its north, while Oman's Musandam Peninsula forms the southern side of the passage.
Tankers and other commercial vessels use this route to reach international markets. Before the war, roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies passed through it.

During the 2026 conflict, shipping attacks, restrictions, and competing military operations disrupted regional movements. Reports described Iranian pressure on the passage and American measures aimed at Iranian shipping.
On November 17, Reuters reported renewed tanker danger near Oman's Khasab and continuing serious disputes over maritime access. Exact conditions change, so every map needs a source date.

Hormuz matters because geography concentrates maritime traffic in a constrained corridor. Can diplomacy restore safer passage for international ships? Share your view below, and follow if you like it.
